before.title: Monopole-dipole expansion with an explicit remainder for compactly supported $L^1$ densities
before.statement: Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$). Let $a>0$ and let $\rho\in L^1(\mathbb R^3)$ vanish outside $\{y:\lvert y\rvert\le a\}$. Put $Q:=\int\rho$, $p:=\int y\,\rho(y)\,dy$ and $\lVert\rho\rVert_1:=\int\lvert\rho\rvert$. Then for every $x$ with $r:=\lvert x\rvert\ge2a>0$, $$\int_{\mathbb R^3}\frac{\rho(y)}{\lvert x-y\rvert}\,dy=\frac Qr+\frac{p\cdot x}{r^3}+R(x),\qquad \lvert R(x)\rvert\le\frac{16\,a^2\lVert\rho\rVert_1}{r^3}.$$
before.strategy: Set $h(s)=\lvert x-sy\rvert^{-1}$; $h$ is $C^2$ on $[0,1]$ and the identity $h(1)-h(0)-h'(0)=\int_0^1(1-s)h''(s)\,ds$ follows from the fundamental theorem applied to $\frac{d}{ds}[(1-s)h'(s)+h(s)]=(1-s)h''(s)$. Because $\lvert x-sy\rvert\ge r-a\ge r/2$ for $r\ge2a$, one has $\lvert h''(s)\rvert\le4\lvert y\rvert^2/(r-a)^3\le32\lvert y\rvert^2/r^3$, and integrating against $\lvert\rho\rvert$ gives the bound with $C=16$, which is permissible but not sharp. The published far-field theorem supplies the leading $Q/r$ term only.

after.title: Monopole-dipole expansion with an explicit remainder for compactly supported $L^1$ densities

before.title: Legendre polynomials from a convergent zonal kernel: generating function and exterior expansion
before.statement: For $z\in[-1,1]$ define the real polynomial $P_l(z)=\pi^{-1}\int_0^\pi\bigl[z+i\sqrt{1-z^2}\,\cos\theta\bigr]^l\,d\theta$, $l\in\mathbb N_0$. Then $P_l$ is a real polynomial of degree at most $l$ with $|P_l(z)|\le1$ on $[-1,1]$, $P_l(1)=1$, and for $|q|<1$ the series $\sum_{l\ge0}q^lP_l(z)$ converges absolutely and uniformly on $[-1,1]$ with $$(1-2qz+q^2)^{-1/2}=\sum_{l=0}^{\infty}q^lP_l(z),$$ where the branch is the analytic square root equal to $1$ at $q=0$ ([[def-series-of-real-functions]], [[thm-weierstrass-m-test-for-function-series]]). Consequently, for $r>|y|$ with $n=x/|x|$ and $N\in\mathbb N_0$, $\bigl|\,|x-y|^{-1}-\sum_{l=0}^{N}|y|^l|x|^{-l-1}P_l(n\cdot y/|y|)\bigr|\le|y|^{N+1}|x|^{-N-2}(1-|y|/|x|)^{-1}$, uniformly on $|y|\le a<r$ (with $y=0$ interpreted by the zero higher terms), and after integrating against an $L^1$ source the corresponding multipole expansion converges with that error times its $L^1$ norm. On an observation compact set disjoint from $\overline{B_a(0)}$ every fixed spatial derivative series converges uniformly, by analyticity of the kernel in the parameter $y$ ([[def-complex-domain]], [[thm-identity-theorem-holomorphic-functions]], [[thm-differentiation-under-the-integral-sign]]). This lemma supplies the convergent zonal kernel; it does not by itself prove a spherical $L^2$ basis or boundary convergence.
before.strategy: Realness and the degree bound follow by expanding the finite power and integrating the odd cosine moments away; $|P_l(z)|\le1$ uses $|z+i\sqrt{1-z^2}\cos\theta|\le1$. For the generating function integrate the geometric series $\sum_{l\ge0}[q(z+i\sqrt{1-z^2}\cos\theta)]^l=(1-qz-iq\sqrt{1-z^2}\cos\theta)^{-1}$ termwise over $\theta$; the geometric ratio has modulus $\le|q|<1$ uniformly in $\theta$, so the Weierstrass $M$-test gives uniform convergence and termwise integration gives the coefficient representation $P_l$. The integral $\int_0^\pi(a+b\cos\theta)^{-1}d\theta=\pi/\sqrt{a^2-b^2}$ for $a>|b|$ is computed by the tangent substitution $u=\tan(\theta/2)$ ([[thm-substitution]], [[thm-principal-inverse-tangent-calculus]]). Substituting $a=1-qz$, $b=-iq\sqrt{1-z^2}$ gives $\pi(1-2qz+q^2)^{-1/2}$. Both sides are holomorphic in $(q,z)$ near the real values with $|q|<1$, where $1-2qz+q^2$ never vanishes, so the identity extends by the identity theorem for holomorphic functions ([[def-complex-domain]], [[thm-identity-theorem-holomorphic-functions]]). Substituting $q=|y|/r$, $z=n\cdot y/|y|$ and using $|P_l|\le1$ gives the geometric tail bound for the displayed kernel expansion. For derivative convergence on a compact observation set, the kernel is holomorphic in a neighbourhood of the parameter domain bounded away from its zeros; Cauchy-type uniform bounds on a slightly larger complex disk ([[thm-differentiation-under-the-integral-sign]]) bound every fixed spatial derivative of the series terms by a polynomial in $l$ times $(a/r)^l$, and the ratio test gives uniform convergence of each derivative series. No asymptotic large-$l$ formula is used.

after.title: Legendre polynomials from a convergent zonal kernel: generating function and exterior expansion
after.statement: For $z\in[-1,1]$ define the real polynomial $P_l(z)=\pi^{-1}\int_0^\pi\bigl[z+i\sqrt{1-z^2}\,\cos\theta\bigr]^l\,d\theta$, $l\in\mathbb N_0$. For the integrated $L^1$-source and every-spatial-derivative assertions, assume Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]) through the Lebesgue and harmonic-estimate interfaces. On an observation compact set disjoint from $\overline{B_a(0)}$ every fixed spatial derivative series converges uniformly, uniformly also over $|y|\le a$, by harmonicity of the coefficient terms and [[thm-interior-derivative-estimates-for-harmonic-functions]]. The initial finite-Riemann polynomial/generating assertions are choice-free. This lemma supplies the convergent zonal kernel; it does not by itself prove a spherical $L^2$ basis or boundary convergence.
after.strategy:
Expand the finite power in the defining Riemann integral: odd cosine powers integrate to zero by the substitution theta to pi-theta, and even powers have factors $(1-z^2)^jz^{l-2j}$, so $P_l$ is a real polynomial, with $P_l(1)=1$ and $|P_l(z)|\le1$. For each FIXED real $z\in[-1,1]$, put $w(\theta)=z+i\sqrt{1-z^2}\cos\theta$; $|w|\le1$, so the geometric series is uniformly convergent on every $|q|\le q_0<1$ and finite-Riemann termwise integration gives $G_z(q)=\sum_lq^lP_l(z)=\pi^{-1}\int_0^\pi(1-qw(\theta))^{-1}d\theta$. The sum is holomorphic on the unit disk by [[thm-termwise-differentiation-of-complex-power-series]]. No holomorphy in z at the endpoints is asserted.

For real $a>|b|$ the tangent substitution gives $I(a,b)=\int_0^\pi(a+b\cos\theta)^{-1}d\theta=\pi/\sqrt{a^2-b^2}$ by [[thm-substitution]] and [[thm-principal-inverse-tangent-calculus]]. Near $(a,b)=(1,0)$ the rational integrand and its first parameter derivatives are uniformly bounded on the compact theta interval, so uniform difference quotients through the finite Riemann integral give holomorphy in each parameter separately. The identity $I(a,b)^2(a^2-b^2)=\pi^2$ first extends in complex a for every fixed small real b, then in complex b for every fixed nearby complex a, by the ONE-variable [[thm-identity-theorem-holomorphic-functions]]. Substitute $a=1-qz$, $b=-iq\sqrt{1-z^2}$ near q0 to get $(1-2qz+q^2)G_z(q)^2=1$. This holomorphic identity extends over the connected unit disk by the same one-variable theorem. Since $G_z(0)=1$, it is exactly the specified analytic inverse-square-root branch. The zeros of the polynomial factor lie on the unit circle for every fixed real z. Substitution q=|y|/r now proves the exterior kernel series and its geometric remainder, including zero y.

Each coefficient $c_l(x,y)=|y|^l|x|^{-l-1}P_l((x/|x|)\cdot(y/|y|))$ is smooth and harmonic in x away from zero. Indeed it equals $1/l!$ times the lth t-derivative at t0 of $|x-ty|^{-1}$, by the proved scalar power series and [[cor-complex-power-series-coefficient-formula]]. On a neighbourhood of any fixed x nonzero and t0 this kernel is smooth and harmonic in x by [[lem-laplace-fundamental-solution-is-harmonic-off-its-pole]]; finite mixed derivative commutation [[thm-clairaut-schwarz-mixed-partials]] makes its t-coefficient harmonic. The corresponding degree-l solid polynomial in y is harmonic in y by the same argument, using $\Delta_y|x-ty|^{-1}=0$ for all sufficiently small real t. This also supplies the solid-harmonic coefficient used by the later addition lemma without a cyclic dependence.

The empty observation compact has a vacuous uniform-convergence claim. Otherwise fix a nonempty compact observation set K with inf_K|x|>a. Choose a positive delta and a bounded closed neighbourhood Kplus of K with every closed delta-ball centred on K contained in Kplus and inf_Kplus|x|>a. The geometric kernel estimate gives a uniform tail bound E_N tending to zero on Kplus times the whole closed source ball |y|<=a. Harmonic partial-sum differences v satisfy the exact [[thm-interior-derivative-estimates-for-harmonic-functions]] bound $|D^\alpha v(x)|\le C_{3,\alpha}\delta^{-3-|\alpha|}\int_{B_\delta(x)}|v|\le C_{3,\alpha}\delta^{-3-|\alpha|}|B_\delta|\sup_{Kplus}|v|$. Thus every spatial derivative is uniformly Cauchy on K, uniformly in y. Uniform derivative limits are identified inductively along short coordinate segments by [[thm-newton-leibniz-with-interior-derivative]], so they are exactly the derivatives of the kernel. Against a compact $L^1$ density, the same bound times |rho| gives an integrable envelope and multiplies each tail by ||rho||1 using [[prop-order-and-scalar-rules-for-the-nonnegative-integral]]. Countable Choice enters only the Lebesgue and harmonic-estimate branches; the initial finite polynomial and scalar generating argument uses no Choice. No multivariable complex Cauchy estimate is invoked. For an actual L1 source choose its representative zero outside the closed source ball. On each small open observation-coordinate interval inside Kplus, every kernel derivative is smooth on the fixed compact source ball and has a uniform finite bound C_alpha; the next derivative integrand is bounded by C_alpha times |rho|, an integrable majorant. Thus [[thm-differentiation-under-the-integral-sign]] applies with zero exceptional set after the off-ball integrand is defined as zero. This identifies all integral derivatives directly as well as by the uniform harmonic-series limit.

before.title: Outgoing source Helmholtz field: fundamental solution, Fraunhofer and Fresnel error terms
before.statement: For $k>0$ define $G_k(x)=e^{ik|x|}/(4\pi|x|)$ off the origin, a locally integrable complex function. Then $$(-\Delta-k^2)G_k=\delta_0$$ distributionally. For a finite complex measure $\alpha$ supported in $B_a(0)$, the field $u=G_k*\alpha$ is smooth outside the support, solves $(\Delta+k^2)u=0$ there and is outgoing: for $x=rn$, $r\ge2a$, $$u(rn)=\frac{e^{ikr}}{4\pi r}\int e^{-ikn\cdot y}\,d\alpha(y)+O\!\Bigl(\frac{\|\alpha\|_{\mathrm{TV}}}{r}\Bigl[\frac{a}{r}+\frac{ka^2}{r}\Bigr]\Bigr)$$ uniformly in direction, and $r(\partial_ru-iku)=O(r^{-1})$ uniformly. For a planar aperture $y=(y_1,y_2,0)$ with observation $x=(\xi_1,\xi_2,z)$, $z>0$, $|\xi|\le b$, $a+b\ll z$, the Fresnel approximation replaces $R=|x-y|$ by $z+|\xi-y|^2/(2z)$ and $1/R$ by $1/z$ with phase error $O(k(a+b)^4/z^3)$ and relative amplitude error $O((a+b)^2/z^2)$, hence absolute field error $O(\|\alpha\|_{\mathrm{TV}}z^{-1}[(a+b)^2/z^2+k(a+b)^4/z^3])$. Aperture data are an explicitly specified scalar source, not asserted to be the unknown exact Maxwell boundary traces, and no uniqueness or existence for arbitrary obstacle boundary data is claimed.
before.strategy: For radial $f(r)$ one has $\Delta f=f''+2f'/r$ by direct coordinate differentiation of $\partial_ir=x_i/r$ ([[def-laplacian-of-a-c2-function]]), and inserting $f=G_k$ gives $(\Delta+k^2)f=0$ for $r>0$. For the distributional identity excise a ball $B_\delta$ inside a compact test integration; the second Green identity ([[cor-second-green-identity-on-a-bounded-c-one-domain]]) on the excised domain cancels the $k^2$ terms and leaves the inner flux, where $G_k=1/(4\pi\delta)+O(1)$ and $\partial_rG_k=-1/(4\pi\delta^2)+O(1)$: the derivative-test boundary term is $O(\delta)$ and the leading unit flux multiplies $\psi(0)$, while the local $k^2G_k$ integral is $O(\delta^2)$; the limit is $\delta_0$ with the displayed sign. Off-support smoothness and all derivatives follow from the positive separation of compact observation and source sets, with differentiation under the source integral. For the Fraunhofer error write $R=|rn-y|$ and use the norm expansion of the cited dipole-remainder technique ([[lem-em-coulomb-dipole-remainder]]): $|R-r+n\cdot y|\le Ca^2/r$ and $|r/R-1|\le Ca/r$; the exponential difference is bounded by $C r^{-1}(a/r+ka^2/r)$ via $|e^{i\theta}-1|\le|\theta|$, and integrating against the total variation of $\alpha$ with the integral triangle inequality ([[thm-integral-triangle-inequality]]) gives the displayed error; the outgoing relation follows from $\partial_rR=1+O(a^2/r^2)$ and $R^{-2}=O(r^{-2})$. The Fresnel estimate is the Taylor expansion of the norm with explicit remainder on the compact small-$s$ region $s=|\xi-y|^2/z^2$, using $|e^{i\theta}-1|\le|\theta|$.

before.title: Spherical harmonics: orthogonal decomposition, complete basis and addition theorem
before.statement: Let $P_l$ denote the real vector space of homogeneous polynomials of degree $l$ on $\mathbb R^3$, $H_l=\ker(\Delta:P_l\to P_{l-2})$ with $P_k=\{0\}$ for $k<0$, and let spherical harmonics of degree $l$ be the restrictions of $H_l$ to $S^2$, with unnormalised surface measure $d\Omega$ of total mass $4\pi$. Then $P_l=H_l\oplus|x|^2P_{l-2}$, $\dim H_l=2l+1$, harmonics of distinct degree are orthogonal in $L^2(S^2,d\Omega)$, and the union over $l$ of the spaces of spherical harmonics admits a complete orthonormal basis of $L^2(S^2,d\Omega)$ ([[def-orthonormal-family-complete-orthonormal-system-and-hilbert-basis]]). For any real orthonormal basis $Y_{lm}$, $m=1,\dots,2l+1$, of degree-$l$ harmonics the addition theorem holds: $$\sum_{m=1}^{2l+1}Y_{lm}(n)Y_{lm}(n')=\frac{2l+1}{4\pi}P_l(n\cdot n'),$$ where $P_l$ is the Legendre polynomial of the convergent zonal kernel lemma ([[lem-em-convergent-legendre-kernel]]). The Laplacian is the Euclidean one ([[def-laplacian-of-a-c2-function]]). This supplies the harmonic decomposition, orthogonality, completeness and exact addition kernel; it does not assert higher boundary regularity.
before.strategy: For homogeneous $Q$ of degree $l-2j$, Euler's identity $x\cdot\nabla Q=(l-2j)Q$ gives $\Delta(r^{2j}Q)=2j(2l-2j+1)r^{2j-2}Q+r^{2j}\Delta Q$; the ansatz $H=\sum_ja_jr^{2j}\Delta^jP$ with $a_0=1$ and $a_j=-a_{j-1}/[2j(2l-2j+1)]$ cancels consecutive coefficients in $\Delta H$, and the final $\Delta^{\lfloor l/2\rfloor+1}P$ vanishes by degree, so $H$ is harmonic and $P-H$ is divisible by $r^2$; recursion gives the decomposition. For homogeneous harmonic $H_l,H_m$ the Green identity on the ball ([[cor-second-green-identity-on-a-bounded-c-one-domain]]) gives $0=\int_{S^2}(H_l\partial_nH_m-H_m\partial_nH_l)=(m-l)\int_{S^2}H_lH_m$, whence orthogonality of distinct degrees; if a harmonic of degree $l$ equalled $r^2Q$, its orthogonality to all lower-degree harmonics would force $\int_{S^2}H_l^2=0$, so $H_l=0$; the monomial count $\dim P_l=(l+1)(l+2)/2$ gives $\dim H_l=2l+1$, and restriction is injective by the same homogeneity argument. For density, continuous functions are dense in $L^2(S^2)$ by a finite smooth graph atlas with subordinate smooth cutoffs, pulling each localised function back, mollifying and using the $L^2$ translation and approximate-identity interfaces ([[lem-complex-translation-and-approximate-identity-interfaces]]); the restricted real polynomial algebra is unital and separates points, so Stone-Weierstrass ([[thm-real-stone-weierstrass-general]]) makes it uniformly dense in $C(S^2)$, and the homogeneous-degree decomposition puts every restriction in the finite span of spherical harmonics, giving $L^2$ density. Finite Gram-Schmidt ([[thm-gram-schmidt-orthonormalisation]]) applied to a fixed ordered monomial elimination basis of each $H_l$ produces the orthonormal bases without an undefined basis selection. For the addition theorem, $K_l(n,n')=\sum_mY_{lm}(n)Y_{lm}(n')$ is independent of the orthonormal basis and rotation-invariant, and for fixed $n'$ it is the unique (up to scale) rotation-invariant homogeneous harmonic polynomial of degree $l$, which is the coefficient $|y|^lP_l(n'\cdot y/|y|)$ of the convergent kernel of the zonal lemma ([[lem-em-convergent-legendre-kernel]]); evaluating the diagonal by integrating $K_l(n,n)$ gives $(2l+1)/(4\pi)$, completing the addition theorem.

before.title: Exact Helmholtz boundary representation with actual traces
before.statement: Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^3$ be a bounded smooth domain, $k>0$, $x\in\Omega$, and let $u$ be a smooth solution of $(-\Delta-k^2)u=f$ on $\Omega$ with $f$ smooth, using the outgoing fundamental solution $G_k$ of the source Helmholtz lemma ([[lem-em-outgoing-source-helmholtz-and-diffraction]], [[def-surface-integral-on-a-compact-c-one-hypersurface]]). For an exterior outgoing solution truncated by a large sphere, the same representation holds with the actual inner boundary traces: the outgoing leading terms of $G_k$ cancel the large-sphere Wronskian integrand at leading order and the remaining compact-observation estimate tends to zero. The $k^2$ terms cancel; the unit-flux inner kernel and the continuous limit of $u$ contribute the $-u(x)$ term from $\int(u\Delta G_k-G_k\Delta u)$, while the volume source contributes $\int G_kf$. Letting $\delta\to0$, the derivative-test inner term is $O(\delta)$ and the flux times $u-u(x)$ tends to zero by continuity, giving the displayed formula with the normalisation and outward-hole sign fixed as in the source lemma ([[lem-em-outgoing-source-helmholtz-and-diffraction]]). accepted_round1_before.title: Exact Helmholtz boundary representation with actual traces
accepted_round1_before.statement:

More generally, retain the justified weaker classical-trace branch: u is C2 inside Omega, u and all first derivatives extend continuously to its closure, f=(-Delta-k²)u belongs to L1(Omega), and the equation holds inside. $$u(x)=\int_\Omega G_k(x-y)f(y)\,dy+\int_{\partial\Omega}\bigl[G_k(x-y)\partial_nu(y)-u(y)\partial_{n_y}G_k(x-y)\bigr]dS_y,$$

$$[l(l+1)]^p c_{lm}=\int_{S^2}(-\Lambda)^pg\,Y_{lm}\,d\Omega,\qquad |c_{lm}|\le\frac{\|\Lambda^pg\|_2}{[l(l+1)]^p}.$$
The smooth g and all these angular derivatives are bounded on the compact sphere and have finite L2 norms. Treat l0 separately as its single finite constant coefficient. The addition diagonal of H2 gives $\|Y_{lm}\|_\infty\le\sqrt{(2l+1)/(4\pi)}$. With p2, the total weighted absolute sum
$$\sum_{l,m}(l+1+2kR_0)|c_{lm}|\,\|Y_{lm}\|_\infty<\infty$$
follows: for l>=1 its degree-l bound is a fixed constant times $(2l+1)(l+1+2kR_0)\sqrt{(2l+1)/(4\pi)}[l(l+1)]^{-2}=O(l^{-3/2})$. This is the actual summability argument for every smooth trace, not an unproved claim of coefficient decay.

Exact radial majorants. From the earlier Hankel proof, $F_l(z)=z^2|h_l(z)|^2=\sum_{j=0}^la_jz^{-2j}$ has a0=1 and positive a_j, so it is nonincreasing in z>0. Consequently, for $\phi_l(r)=h_l(kr)/h_l(kR_0)$,

before.title: Exterior spherical multipole expansion and the ball boundary series
before.statement:
Let $a>0$ and let $\rho\in L^1(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb R)$ vanish outside $\overline B_a(0)$. Use the complete orthonormal basis $\{Y_{lm}\}$ of real spherical harmonics on $S^2$ with unnormalised surface measure $d\sigma$ of total mass $4\pi$ and the addition theorem of [[lem-em-spherical-harmonic-basis-and-addition]], and the Legendre generating kernel and its compact remainder bound from [[lem-em-convergent-legendre-kernel]]. Write $x=rn$, $r=|x|$, $n\in S^2$. Then:
(a) **Exterior multipole expansion.** For every $x$ with $|x|>a$,
$$\int_{\mathbb R^3}\frac{\rho(y)}{|x-y|}\,dy=\sum_{l=0}^\infty\sum_{m=1}^{2l+1}\frac{4\pi}{2l+1}\frac{Y_{lm}(n)}{r^{l+1}}\int_{\mathbb R^3}|y|^lY_{lm}(y/|y|)\rho(y)\,dy,$$
the series converging absolutely and uniformly on $\{|x|\ge r_0\}$ for every $r_0>a$, with tail after degree $N$ bounded by $\|\rho\|_1\,a^{N+1}/(r_0^{N+2}(1-a/r_0))$; the degree-$l$ term is the $L^2(S^2)$ projection of $y\mapsto|x-y|^{-1}\rho(y)$ onto the degree-$l$ harmonics. The degree-zero and degree-one terms are the Coulomb and dipole terms with the explicit remainder bound of [[lem-em-coulomb-dipole-remainder]] ($Q=\int\rho$, $p=\int y\rho(y)\,dy$, $|R(x)|\le16a^2\|\rho\|_1/|x|^3$ for $|x|\ge2a$).
(b) **Termwise differentiation.** On every compact $K$ with $\inf_K|x|>a$ the series may be differentiated termwise to every order, the differentiated series converging uniformly on $K$; in particular the potential is $C^\infty$ on $\{|x|>a\}$.
(c) **Ball boundary branch.** For $f\in L^2(S^2)$ with coefficients $f_{lm}$ the series $u(rn)=\sum_{l,m}r^lf_{lm}Y_{lm}(n)$ converges in $L^2(S^2)$ as $r\uparrow1$ and, with all derivatives, uniformly on each closed ball of radius $<1$, is harmonic on the open unit ball, and is the unique harmonic function there with a finite $\sup_{r<1}\|u(r\cdot)\|_2$ and $L^2$ boundary limit $f$; for continuous $f$ it equals the Poisson integral $(1-r^2)/(4\pi|rn-n'|^3)$ of $f$ and extends continuously to the closed ball with boundary values $f$. before.statement: Three exact boundary checks. (i) The sphere trace $f(n)=n_3$ is the trace of the homogeneous degree-one harmonic polynomial $u(x)=x_3$, so the ball boundary branch of [[thm-em-spherical-multipole-basis]] applies to it; the simultaneous conditions $\Delta u=0$ in the unit ball $B_1$ and $\partial_nu=1$ on $S^2$ are incompatible, because the divergence theorem gives $0=\int_{B_1}\Delta u\,dx=\int_{S^2}\partial_nu\,d\sigma=\sigma(S^2)=4\pi$. (ii) For the coefficient $\varepsilon=1$ on $\{x_1<0\}$ and $\varepsilon=2$ on $\{x_1>0\}$, the function $u=x_1$ on the first side and $u=x_1/2$ on the second is continuous and locally $H^1$, and $\varepsilon\partial_1u\equiv1$, so $-\operatorname{div}(\varepsilon\nabla u)=0$ weakly although $u$ is not $C^1$: its first derivative jumps from $1$ to $1/2$ across the interface. Hence the smooth-coefficient statements of [[thm-em-elliptic-boundary-existence]] cannot be extended to this piecewise-constant case, and the correct conclusion there is the piecewise regularity recorded by that item, not a global $C^1$ or $C^\infty$-on-the-closure statement. (iii) The same wild-coefficient configuration is a hypothesis boundary for the smooth-domain spectral completeness of [[thm-em-waveguide-spectral-completeness]]: its coefficients and interfaces are exactly the ones excluded from the smooth $C^\infty$ PEC/smooth-domain hypotheses, and the explicit solution shows that a global classical conclusion fails while the weak $H^1$ formulation remains valid. All three parts are exact finite computations or classical divergence-theorem evaluations; they assert no physical interpretation.

before.title: Total charge, dipole moment, Cartesian moments and traceless quadrupole of a static charge distribution
before.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$), inherited from the Lebesgue interface used below ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let the laboratory region, its chart, its spatial Euclidean structure and its units be those of [[def-em-lab-geometry]] and [[def-em-si-conventions]], and let $\delta_{ij}$ be the Kronecker symbol in the $\delta$-orthonormal basis $(e_1,e_2,e_3)$ of the frame, with $|y|$ the Euclidean norm of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. This definition assigns **source moments** to a static charge distribution in the fixed-time reading of [[def-em-electrostatic-regime]] (d) and (e). Two branches are declared.

(a) [Absolutely continuous branch] Let $a>0$ and let $\rho\in L^1(\mathbb R^3)$ be real ([[def-l-one-of-a-measure]]) and vanish $\lambda_3$-almost everywhere outside the closed ball $\overline B_a(0)=\{y:|y|\le a\}$ ([[def-metric-ball]], [[def-measure-null-set-and-almost-everywhere]]). The **total charge** $Q$, the **dipole moment** $p$, the **degree-$l$ Cartesian moments** $M_{i_1\dots i_l}$ and the **traceless quadrupole** $Q_{ij}$ are
$$Q:=\int_{\mathbb R^3}\rho\,d\lambda_3,\qquad p_i:=\int_{\mathbb R^3}y_i\,\rho(y)\,d\lambda_3(y),$$
$$M_{i_1\dots i_l}:=\int_{\mathbb R^3}y_{i_1}\cdots y_{i_l}\,\rho(y)\,d\lambda_3(y)\quad(l\ge0),\qquad Q_{ij}:=\int_{\mathbb R^3}\bigl(3y_iy_j-|y|^2\delta_{ij}\bigr)\rho(y)\,d\lambda_3(y),$$

before.title: Origin shift of the source moments: $Q$, the dipole $p-Qb$, the Cartesian expansion and the traceless quadrupole
before.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$), inherited from the Lebesgue interface ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $a>0$ and let $\rho\in L^1(\mathbb R^3)$ be real and vanish $\lambda_3$-a.e. outside $\overline B_a(0)$, or let $(x_k,q_k)_{k=1}^N$ be a finite system of stationary point charges, with the source moments of [[def-em-electric-moments]] branches (a) and (c) respectively. For $b\in\mathbb R^3$ define the moments **about the reference point $b$** by replacing, in each integrand of [[def-em-electric-moments]] (a) and in each summand of (c), the vector $y$ by $y-b$ (respectively $x_k$ by $x_k-b$):
$$Q^{(b)}:=\int_{\mathbb R^3}\rho\,d\lambda_3,\quad p^{(b)}:=\int_{\mathbb R^3}(y-b)\,\rho(y)\,d\lambda_3(y),\quad M^{(b)}_{i_1\dots i_l}:=\int_{\mathbb R^3}\prod_{r=1}^l(y-b)_{i_r}\,\rho(y)\,d\lambda_3(y),$$
$$Q^{(b)}_{ij}:=\int_{\mathbb R^3}\bigl(3(y-b)_i(y-b)_j-|y-b|^2\delta_{ij}\bigr)\rho(y)\,d\lambda_3(y),$$
and analogously with finite sums $M^{(b)}_{i_1\dots i_l}=\sum_{k=1}^N q_k\prod_{r=1}^l(x_k-b)_{i_r}$ in the point-charge branch. Every displayed integral is absolutely convergent: $\lambda_3$-a.e. on the support the monomials obey $|y_{i_1}\cdots y_{i_l}|\le a^l$ and, for $y-b$, $|y-b|^l\le(|y|+|b|)^l$ and $|3(y-b)_i(y-b)_j-|y-b|^2\delta_{ij}|\le4(|y|+|b|)^2$, so the integrands are dominated by constants times $|\rho|\in L^1$ ([[def-em-electric-moments]] (a), [[thm-integral-triangle-inequality]], [[thm-monotonicity-of-the-integral]], [[prop-order-and-scalar-rules-for-the-nonnegative-integral]]). Then:
(a) $Q^{(b)}=Q$ for every $b$;
(b) $p^{(b)}=p-Qb$, so the dipole moment is independent of the reference point exactly when $Q=0$;
(c) for every $l\ge0$,
$$M^{(b)}_{i_1\dots i_l}=\sum_{S\subseteq\{1,\dots,l\}}(-1)^{|S|}\Bigl(\prod_{r\in S}b_{i_r}\Bigr)M_{(i_r:\,r\notin S)},$$
where $M_{(i_r:\,r\notin S)}$ is the Cartesian moment whose index list is the complement of $S$ and the empty index list is read as $Q$; in particular
$$M^{(b)}_{ij}=M_{ij}-b_ip_j-b_jp_i+b_ib_jQ;$$
(d) $Q^{(b)}_{ij}=Q_{ij}-3\bigl(b_ip_j+b_jp_i\bigr)+2(b\cdot p)\delta_{ij}+\bigl(3b_ib_j-|b|^2\delta_{ij}\bigr)Q$; consequently, if $Q=0$ and $p=0$, then $Q^{(b)}_{ij}=Q_{ij}$ for every $b$ (the traceless quadrupole of a neutral, non-dipolar distribution is independent of the reference point);

The theorem is the expansion of the polynomial $\prod_{r=1}^l(y_{i_r}-b_{i_r})$ followed by termwise integration (or summation). For (a) and (b) the degrees $0$ and $1$ are immediate; constant multiples of $\rho$ and of $y_i\rho$ pass through the integral by linearity of the Lebesgue integral on $L^1$ ([[thm-linearity-of-the-lebesgue-integral-on-l-one]]), and the finite-sum branch by linearity of finite sums ([[def-finite-sum]], [[lem-finite-sum-laws]]). $$\prod_{r=1}^l(y_{i_r}-b_{i_r})=\sum_{S\subseteq\{1,\dots,l\}}(-1)^{|S|}\Bigl(\prod_{r\in S}b_{i_r}\Bigr)\Bigl(\prod_{r\notin S}y_{i_r}\Bigr),$$

after.title: External force and torque on a small neutral charge distribution in a slowly varying electrostatic field
after.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$), inherited from the Lebesgue interface ([[def-countable-choice]]). Consider the matter model in which the prescribed static distribution $\rho$ is carried by a body at rest in the laboratory frame and adopt additionally the prescribed external force model $f_{\mathrm{ext}}=\rho E_{\mathrm{ext}}$. This is a declared extension to these locally integrable charge data and Lipschitz fields, motivated by the smooth continuum coupling of [[post-em-lorentz-coupling]] (ii); that postulate covers smooth sources and does not itself establish this extension. The only force counted by the present model is $f_{\mathrm{ext}}$; the self-field of $\rho$, all other fields, mechanical support and back-reaction are excluded by this model. Define the **total external force** and the **total external torque about the origin** by the componentwise Lebesgue integrals
$$F:=\int_{\mathbb R^3}\rho(y)\,E_{\mathrm{ext}}(y)\,d\lambda_3(y)\in\mathbb R^3,\qquad \tau:=\int_{\mathbb R^3}\rho(y)\,\bigl(y\times E_{\mathrm{ext}}(y)\bigr)\,d\lambda_3(y)\in\mathbb R^3,$$
absolutely convergent because on the support $|E_{\mathrm{ext}}|\le|E_{\mathrm{ext}}(0)|+La$ and $|y\times E_{\mathrm{ext}}|\le a(|E_{\mathrm{ext}}(0)|+La)$, so each component is dominated by a constant times $|\rho|\in L^1$ ([[def-integral-over-a-measurable-set]], [[def-integrable-real-and-complex-functions-and-their-integrals]], [[def-cross-product-in-r3]], [[thm-cross-product-norm-is-the-two-vector-gram-determinant]], [[thm-integral-triangle-inequality]], [[prop-order-and-scalar-rules-for-the-nonnegative-integral]]). Then:
(a) [Uniform force and torque expansions]
$$F=Q\,E_{\mathrm{ext}}(0)+R_F,\qquad |R_F|\le L\,a\,\|\rho\|_1,\qquad \tau=p\times E_{\mathrm{ext}}(0)+R_\tau,\qquad |R_\tau|\le L\,a^2\|\rho\|_1,$$
where $Q$ and $p$ are the total charge and dipole moment of [[def-em-electric-moments]] (a) and $\|\rho\|_1=\int|\rho|\,d\lambda_3$;
(b) [Neutral distribution] if $Q=0$ then the leading force term vanishes, $F=R_F$ with $|R_F|\le La\|\rho\|_1$, and the torque is the ideal-dipole torque $p\times E_{\mathrm{ext}}(0)$ up to the bound $|R_\tau|\le La^2\|\rho\|_1$; in this sense a neutral distribution of size $a$ in a field with Lipschitz constant $L$ carries the dipole torque $p\times E_{\mathrm{ext}}(0)$ with an explicit remainder;
(c) [Reference-point shift] for any reference point $o\in\mathbb R^3$, the torque about $o$, $\tau_o:=\int_{\mathbb R^3}\rho(y)\,(y-o)\times E_{\mathrm{ext}}(y)\,d\lambda_3(y)$, equals $\tau-o\times F$ exactly;
(d) [Ideal pair of test charges at rest] let $q\in\mathbb R$ and $d\in\mathbb R^3\setminus\{0\}$, put $a=|d|/2$, and consider the two stationary point charges $+q$ at $d/2$ and $-q$ at $-d/2$ ([[def-em-electric-moments]] (c)), each treated as a test charge at rest in the laboratory chart in the same prescribed external field $E_{\mathrm{ext}}$, with the mutual interaction and the self-field of each charge excluded by the model. Adopt for this finite prescribed-charge branch the external force assignment $F_k=q_kE_{\rm ext}(x_k)$ and torque $x_k\times F_k$. It is defined for merely continuous external field values at the two points, independently of a worldline equation. For the same Lipschitz bound as above, finite summation gives the expansions of (a),(b), with Q0, p=qd, and total variation2|q|: $|R_F|\le2|q|La$, $|R_\tau|\le2|q|La^2$. More generally the exact finite force/torque sum requires only the specified field values; no Lipschitz estimate is asserted without its hypothesis.

(d1) [Covariant sufficient specialization] If, in addition, an actual prescribed electromagnetic tensor $F$ of [[def-em-electromagnetic-tensor]] is $C^1$ on a neighbourhood of the graph of each massive future-timelike $C^2$ test worldline with constant charge qprime and supplied rest mass m>0, and the external-field coupling [[post-em-lorentz-coupling]](i) applies, then at an instant with zero coordinate velocity $U=(c,0,0,0)$ its spatial force is $q'E_{\rm ext}$, because $U_0=-c$ and $F^{i0}=-E_i/c$. This reproduces the prescribed point-force assignment at that instant. Similarly the smooth-source $J=0$ matter-coupling branch of postulate(ii) reproduces the continuum force assignment when its own source/field/matter hypotheses hold. No C1 tensor or worldline is inferred from merely continuous E data, and no two-charge trajectory existence or permanent rest is claimed.

(e) [Scope] the statement is conditional on the explicitly stated matter model: only the prescribed external field acts on the distribution, the distribution is prescribed and at rest, and no self-force, back-reaction, mechanical equilibrium, stability or dynamics of the body is asserted; the external field is a datum, not solved for. Clause (d) is an instantaneous idealisation of two ideal point test charges with mutual interaction excluded; it is not a two-body dynamics, a bound-state or a stability statement. No radiation, medium response or empirical claim is made. The prescribed finite force assignment and finite moment algebra in(d) are choice-free; the volume integrals in(a)-(c) carry their explicit measure premise, while(d1) is a separate conditional instantiation of the exact physical coupling.

before.title: Uniform Coulomb dipole expansion of a compactly supported charge density with an explicit remainder
before.strategy: First, for $|x|\ge2a$ and $\lambda_3$-a.e. $y$ one has $\rho(y)=0$ off $\overline B_a(0)$, while for $y\in\overline B_a(0)$ one has $|x-y|\ge r-a\ge r/2>0$ ([[lem-every-norm-on-rn-is-continuous-for-the-euclidean-metric]], [[def-metric-ball]], [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]); hence $|x-y|^{-1}\le2/r$ on the support and the integral against $\rho$ converges absolutely ([[thm-integral-triangle-inequality]], [[thm-monotonicity-of-the-integral]], [[prop-order-and-scalar-rules-for-the-nonnegative-integral]], [[def-integral-over-a-measurable-set]], [[def-integrable-real-and-complex-functions-and-their-integrals]]). Since the kernel is bounded on the support and the support is $\lambda_3$-a.e. contained in $\overline B_a(0)$, the integral equals $N\rho(x)$ by the defining formula of [[def-newtonian-potential]] ([[thm-the-lebesgue-integral-respects-almost-everywhere-equality]]). Because $\Phi(z)=1/(4\pi|z|)$ for $n=3$ ([[pthm-em-coulomb-solution]] (c)), one has $N\rho(x)=(4\pi)^{-1}\int_{\mathbb R^3}\rho(y)|x-y|^{-1}\,d\lambda_3(y)$ and hence $\varphi(x)=(4\pi\varepsilon_0)^{-1}\int_{\mathbb R^3}\rho(y)|x-y|^{-1}\,d\lambda_3(y)$ for $r\ge2a$. Nothing at $r<2a$ is asserted, because the kernel singularity may meet the support there; the proof uses no differentiation of the remainder. For (b), $|p\cdot x|\le|p|\,|x|$ by Cauchy-Schwarz for the Euclidean inner product ([[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]]), so $|p\cdot x|/r^3\le|p|/r^2$, and the triangle inequality for the modulus completes the estimate. after.physical_scope: The exterior potential of a compactly supported $L^1$ charge density in classical electrostatics: for $|x|\ge2a$ the localised Newtonian potential equals the monopole term plus the dipole term plus an explicit remainder bounded by $16a^2\|\rho\|_1/(4\pi\varepsilon_0|x|^3)$, uniformly in the exterior region. before.title: Convergent all-order spherical multipole expansion with monopole, dipole and quadrupole terms
before.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$), inherited from the cited Lebesgue, spherical-harmonic and Newtonian interfaces ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $a>0$ and let $\rho\in L^1(\mathbb R^3)$ be real and vanish $\lambda_3$-a.e. outside $\overline B_a(0)$ ([[def-metric-ball]], [[def-measure-null-set-and-almost-everywhere]]); let $Q$, $p$ and $Q_{ij}$ be the total charge, dipole moment and traceless quadrupole of $\rho$ about the chart origin ([[def-em-electric-moments]] (a)); let $\varphi:=\varepsilon_0^{-1}N\rho$ be the potential of [[pthm-em-coulomb-solution]] (c) with the constants of [[def-em-si-conventions]]; and let $\{Y_{lm}:l\ge0,\ m=1,\dots,2l+1\}$ be a real orthonormal basis of spherical harmonics of $L^2(S^2,d\sigma)$ of degree $l$, with $d\sigma$ the surface measure of total mass $4\pi$ and the addition theorem of [[lem-em-spherical-harmonic-basis-and-addition]] ([[def-orthonormal-family-complete-orthonormal-system-and-hilbert-basis]], [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]). For every $l,m$ define the **spherical multipole moment of degree $l$**
$$q_{lm}:=\int_{\mathbb R^3}|y|^l\,Y_{lm}(y/|y|)\,\rho(y)\,d\lambda_3(y),$$
absolutely convergent because $|Y_{lm}|\le((2l+1)/(4\pi))^{1/2}$ on $S^2$ by the addition theorem and $|y|\le a$ $\lambda_3$-a.e. on the support, so the integrand is dominated by $a^l((2l+1)/(4\pi))^{1/2}|\rho|$ ([[thm-integral-triangle-inequality]], [[thm-monotonicity-of-the-integral]], [[prop-order-and-scalar-rules-for-the-nonnegative-integral]]). Write $x=rn$ with $r=|x|$ and $n\in S^2$. Then:
(a) [Exterior spherical multipole expansion] for every $x$ with $r>a$,
$$\varphi(x)=\frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\sum_{l=0}^{\infty}\sum_{m=1}^{2l+1}\frac{4\pi}{2l+1}\,\frac{Y_{lm}(n)}{r^{l+1}}\,q_{lm},$$
the series converging absolutely and uniformly on $\{|x|\ge r_0\}$ for every $r_0>a$, with the tail after degree $N$ bounded by
$$\Bigl\|\,\varphi-\frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\sum_{l=0}^{N}\sum_{m=1}^{2l+1}\frac{4\pi}{2l+1}\frac{Y_{lm}(n)}{r^{l+1}}q_{lm}\Bigr\|_{\infty,\{|x|\ge r_0\}}\le\frac{\|\rho\|_1\,a^{N+1}}{4\pi\varepsilon_0\,r_0^{N+2}\,(1-a/r_0)};$$
(b) [Monopole, dipole and quadrupole terms] the degree-$0$ and degree-$1$ terms of (a) are the monopole and dipole terms $Q/(4\pi\varepsilon_0r)$ and $p\cdot x/(4\pi\varepsilon_0r^3)$, and for $r\ge2a$ the difference between $\varphi$ and the truncation after degree $1$ obeys the remainder bound of [[pthm-em-electric-dipole-expansion]]; the degree-$2$ term equals the traceless-quadrupole term
$$\frac{1}{8\pi\varepsilon_0r^3}\,n_iQ_{ij}n_j;$$
(c) [Regularity and termwise differentiation] $\varphi$ is of class $C^\infty$ on $\{|x|>a\}$, the series in (a) may be differentiated termwise to every order, the differentiated series converging uniformly on every compact subset of $\{|x|>a\}$; in particular the field $E:=-\nabla\varphi$ of [[def-em-fields]] equals $-\frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\sum_{l,m}\frac{4\pi}{2l+1}\nabla_x\bigl(Y_{lm}(n)r^{-l-1}\bigr)q_{lm}$ on $\{|x|>a\}$, with the same uniform convergence on compact subsets;
(d) [Scope] the hypotheses are a real compactly supported $L^1$ density and the exterior region $r>a$; no claim is made on or inside $\overline B_a(0)$, no convergence at $r=a$ is asserted, the theorem is not asserted for point or singular sources, and no empirical content is involved. The expansion is the exterior expansion of the potential of the static source $\rho$ read in the fixed-time dictionary of [[def-em-electrostatic-regime]] (e).
before.strategy:
Scale the spherical multipole expansion of [[thm-em-spherical-multipole-basis]] (a)-(b) by the constant $(4\pi\varepsilon_0)^{-1}$, exactly as in [[pthm-em-electric-dipole-expansion]]: since $N\rho(x)=(4\pi)^{-1}\int\rho(y)|x-y|^{-1}d\lambda_3(y)$ for the observation points considered, $\varphi=(4\pi\varepsilon_0)^{-1}\int\rho(y)|x-y|^{-1}d\lambda_3(y)$, and part (a) of the supplier gives the displayed series, its absolute and uniform convergence on exterior regions, and the stated tail bound, all multiplied by the constant $(4\pi\varepsilon_0)^{-1}$ ([[thm-linearity-of-the-lebesgue-integral-on-l-one]] for scaling the integral, [[def-integral-over-a-measurable-set]], [[def-integrable-real-and-complex-functions-and-their-integrals]]). The coefficients $q_{lm}$ are absolutely convergent by the addition theorem's bound $\sum_{m=1}^{2l+1}Y_{lm}(n)^2=(2l+1)/(4\pi)$ of [[lem-em-spherical-harmonic-basis-and-addition]], which gives $|Y_{lm}|\le((2l+1)/(4\pi))^{1/2}$, and by $|y|\le a$ on the support ([[def-orthonormal-family-complete-orthonormal-system-and-hilbert-basis]]). $$\sum_{m=1}^{5}Y_{2m}(n)q_{2m}=\frac{5}{4\pi}\int_{\mathbb R^3}|y|^2P_2\Bigl(n\cdot\frac{y}{|y|}\Bigr)\rho(y)\,d\lambda_3(y),$$
and the second Legendre polynomial is fixed by the defining identity $(1-2qz+q^2)^{-1/2}=\sum_{l\ge0}q^lP_l(z)$ of [[lem-em-convergent-legendre-kernel]]: the coefficient of $q^2$ in the Taylor expansion of the left side at $q=0$ is $\frac12\frac{d^2}{dq^2}(1-2qz+q^2)^{-1/2}\big|_{q=0}=\frac{3z^2-1}{2}$ (the first and second derivatives computed by the chain rule, [[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]], [[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]], [[thm-real-power-continuity-and-derivatives]]), while that coefficient on the right side is $P_2(z)$ (uniqueness of Taylor coefficients, [[def-taylor-polynomial-and-remainder]], [[lem-taylor-polynomial-derivatives]]); hence $P_2(z)=(3z^2-1)/2$. $$\sum_{m=1}^{5}Y_{2m}(n)q_{2m}=\frac{5}{8\pi}\int_{\mathbb R^3}\bigl(3(n\cdot y)^2-|y|^2\bigr)\rho(y)\,d\lambda_3(y)=\frac{5}{8\pi}\,n_iQ_{ij}n_j$$
by the definition of $Q_{ij}$ in [[def-em-electric-moments]] (a) and linearity of the integral; the degree-$2$ term of (a) is then $\frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\cdot\frac{4\pi}{5}\cdot\frac{1}{r^3}\cdot\frac{5}{8\pi}n_iQ_{ij}n_j=\frac{n_iQ_{ij}n_j}{8\pi\varepsilon_0r^3}$. For (c): part (b) of [[thm-em-spherical-multipole-basis]] gives that $\varphi$ is $C^\infty$ on $\{|x|>a\}$ and that the series may be differentiated termwise to every order with uniform convergence of each differentiated series on compact subsets; the displayed field series is the termwise gradient, with [[def-em-fields]] for the field object. The fixed-time dictionary is [[def-em-electrostatic-regime]] (e). All estimates use the triangle and monotonicity rules for the Lebesgue integral ([[thm-integral-triangle-inequality]], [[thm-monotonicity-of-the-integral]], [[prop-order-and-scalar-rules-for-the-nonnegative-integral]]), the $\lambda_3$-a.e. support convention ([[def-measure-null-set-and-almost-everywhere]], [[thm-the-lebesgue-integral-respects-almost-everywhere-equality]]) and the declared Countable Choice of the measure, harmonic and Newtonian interfaces; no convergence at $r=a$ and no point-source assertion is made.

before.title: Exact two-charge dipole potential, its moments and the explicit far-field remainder
before.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$), inherited from the cited distribution and Lebesgue interfaces ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $q\in\mathbb R$ and $d\in\mathbb R^3\setminus\{0\}$, put $a:=|d|/2$, and let the source be the two stationary point charges $+q$ at $d/2$ and $-q$ at $-d/2$ (charge parameters in coulombs and the constant $\varepsilon_0$ of [[def-em-si-conventions]]), with fixed-time reading $q\delta_{d/2}-q\delta_{-d/2}$ ([[def-em-electrostatic-regime]] (e), [[def-dirac-delta-and-its-derivatives]]). Define, with arbitrary values at the two points,
$$\varphi(x):=\frac{q}{4\pi\varepsilon_0|x-d/2|}-\frac{q}{4\pi\varepsilon_0|x+d/2|}\qquad\bigl(x\notin\{d/2,-d/2\}\bigr).$$
Then:
(a) [Exact potential and equations] $\varphi$ is locally integrable on $\mathbb R^3$ and of class $C^\infty$ on $\mathbb R^3\setminus\{d/2,-d/2\}$; with $E:=-\nabla\varphi$ on that set ([[def-em-fields]]), the pair $(E,0)$ satisfies the distributional pure electrostatic equations
$$\operatorname{div}E=\frac{q\,\delta_{d/2}-q\,\delta_{-d/2}}{\varepsilon_0},\qquad \operatorname{curl}E=0\qquad\text{in }\mathcal D'(\mathbb R^3)$$
